reminder: A semiprime ring has no nonzero [nilpotent ideal](c:nilpotent-ideal).
definition: A [ring](c:ring) $R$ is semiprime when it has no nonzero [nilpotent ideal](c:nilpotent-ideal), that is, every two-sided [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ with $I^2=0$ is the zero ideal. Equivalently, $aRa=0$ implies $a=0$ for every $a\in R$.
examples: The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ is semiprime, because it has no nonzero nilpotent element and so no nonzero nilpotent ideal.
Every matrix ring $M_n(F)$ over a field $F$ is semiprime; it is even simple.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ is not semiprime, because its ideal $2\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ is nonzero and squares to zero.

steps: Take a prime ring $R$: for ideals $I$ and $J$, the equation $IJ=0$ forces $I=0$ or $J=0$.
Let $I$ be an ideal with $I^2=0$.
Apply primeness with $J=I$ to get $I=0$.
So $R$ has no nonzero nilpotent ideal, and $R$ is semiprime.
links.why: Every theorem about semiprime rings also covers all prime rings.

steps: Take a reduced ring $R$, which has no nonzero nilpotent element.
Let $I$ be an ideal with $I^2=0$.
Each $a\in I$ satisfies $a^2\in I^2=0$, so $a=0$.
Hence $I=0$, and $R$ is semiprime.
links.why: Fields and other reduced rings fall under results for semiprime rings.

reminder: A slow manifold is an invariant manifold of a fast-slow system on which the motion is slow.
definition: Take a fast-slow system $\varepsilon\dot x=f(x,y,\varepsilon)$, $\dot y=g(x,y,\varepsilon)$ with small $\varepsilon>0$, which is a [singular perturbation](c:singular-perturbation) of a [dynamical system](c:dynamical-system). A slow manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) that the flow leaves [invariant](c:invariant-set) and that lies within distance $O(\varepsilon)$ of the critical manifold $\{f(x,y,0)=0\}$.
examples: For $\varepsilon\dot x=y-x$, $\dot y=1$, the critical manifold is the line $x=y$ and the line $x=y-\varepsilon$ is a slow manifold.
In the van der Pol system $\varepsilon\dot x=y-x^3/3+x$, $\dot y=-x$, slow manifolds lie near the attracting branches $|x|>1$ of the cubic critical manifold.
Non-example: a trajectory that jumps quickly between two branches of the critical manifold does not lie on a slow manifold.

steps: Take a slow manifold $M_\varepsilon$ of the system.
The flow maps every trajectory that starts in $M_\varepsilon$ to a trajectory inside $M_\varepsilon$.
So $M_\varepsilon$ is an invariant set of the flow.
A slow manifold adds two conditions: it is a manifold, and it stays near the critical manifold.
links.why: A slow manifold is an invariant set, so invariance arguments apply to it.

reminder: A starlike function maps the unit disc one-to-one onto a domain that is star-shaped about the origin.
definition: A [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) $\mathbb{D}$ with $f(0)=0$ is starlike when it is [univalent](c:univalent-function) and its image $f(\mathbb{D})$ is a [star-shaped domain](c:star-domain) about $0$: for each $w\in f(\mathbb{D})$, the segment from $0$ to $w$ lies in $f(\mathbb{D})$. For normalized $f$ with $f'(0)=1$, this holds exactly when $\operatorname{Re}\big(zf'(z)/f(z)\big)>0$ on $\mathbb{D}$.
examples: The Koebe function $k(z)=z/(1-z)^2$ is starlike: it maps $\mathbb{D}$ onto the plane minus the slit $(-\infty,-1/4]$.
The map $f(z)=z/(1-z)$ is starlike: it maps $\mathbb{D}$ onto the convex half-plane $\operatorname{Re}w>-1/2$.

Non-example: a conformal map of $\mathbb{D}$ onto the plane minus the ray $\{i+t: t\ge 0\}$, with $f(0)=0$, is univalent but not starlike, because the segment from $0$ to $1+2i$ meets the removed ray.

steps: Take a starlike function $f$ on the unit disc.
By definition $f$ is holomorphic and one-to-one, so $f$ is univalent.
A starlike function adds two conditions: $f(0)=0$, and the image $f(\mathbb{D})$ is star-shaped about $0$.
links.why: Results about univalent functions apply to starlike functions, which are an important subclass.

reminder: The Steiner inellipse is the one ellipse inside a triangle that touches each side at its midpoint.
definition: For a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, the Steiner inellipse is the unique ellipse, a [conic section](c:conic-section), that lies inside the triangle and is tangent to each side at the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of that side. Its center is the [centroid](c:centroid) of the triangle.
examples: In an equilateral triangle, the Steiner inellipse is the [incircle](c:incircle).
For the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$, the Steiner inellipse touches the sides at $(1/2,0)$, $(0,1/2)$ and $(1/2,1/2)$.
By Marden's theorem, the foci of the Steiner inellipse are the roots of $p'$, where the cubic $p$ has the vertices as roots.
Non-example: in a scalene triangle, the incircle is not the Steiner inellipse, because it does not touch every side at its midpoint.

steps: Take the Steiner inellipse of a triangle $ABC$.
It is an ellipse, and every ellipse is a conic section.
The extra conditions are that it lies inside $ABC$ and touches each side at its midpoint.
links.why: Facts about ellipses and conics apply to the Steiner inellipse.

reminder: A supersymmetry is an invariance under the action of a supergroup, or infinitesimally of a super Lie algebra.
definition: A supersymmetry of a system is an invariance under an action of a [supergroup](c:supergroup) or, infinitesimally, of a [super Lie algebra](c:super-lie-algebra), which extends a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) by odd generators. A proper supersymmetry has a nonzero odd part, which exchanges even (bosonic) and odd (fermionic) variables, and it generalizes the invariance under a [group action](c:group-action) of an ordinary symmetry.
examples: The super-Poincare algebra has odd generators $Q$ with $\{Q,Q\}$ equal to a translation; invariance of an action under it is the supersymmetry of particle physics.
A supersymmetric quantum mechanics has a supercharge $Q$ with $Q^2=H$, where $H$ is the Hamiltonian.
Non-example: invariance under rotations has no odd generators and never mixes bosons with fermions, so it is an ordinary symmetry, not a proper supersymmetry.

steps: Take a group $G$ acting on a space $X$.
View $G$ as a supergroup whose odd part is zero.
View $X$ as a supermanifold whose odd coordinates are zero.
The action is then a supergroup action with no odd generators, so ordinary symmetry is the special case of supersymmetry.
links.why: This shows supersymmetry as an extension of ordinary symmetry, with every old symmetry kept.

reminder: Two tangent [circles](c:circle) meet in exactly one point.
definition: Two [circles](c:circle) in the plane are tangent when they meet in exactly one point. With radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ and distance $d$ between the centers, this means $d=r_1+r_2$ (external tangency) or $d=|r_1-r_2|>0$ (internal tangency).
examples: The circles of radius $1$ with centers $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$ touch at the point $(1,0)$.
The circles of radius $3$ and $1$ with centers $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$ are tangent internally at $(3,0)$.
Non-example: the circles of radius $1$ with centers $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ meet in two points, so they are not tangent.

reminder: A transitive group can move every point of the set to every other point.
definition: A [permutation group](c:permutation-group) $G$ on a set $X$ is transitive when for all $x,y\in X$ some $g\in G$ satisfies $g(x)=y$. Equivalently, the [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ on $X$ has exactly one [orbit](c:orbit).
examples: The symmetric group $S_n$ is transitive on $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
The rotation group of a regular $n$-gon is transitive on the $n$ vertices.
Non-example: the group $\{e,(12),(34),(12)(34)\}$ acting on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is not transitive, because no element moves $1$ to $3$.

steps: Take a primitive permutation group $G$ on $X$.
By definition $G$ is transitive and preserves no block system except the trivial ones.
Forget the condition on block systems.
What remains is a transitive group, so every primitive group is transitive.
links.why: Transitivity is the first, weaker condition in the ladder up to primitivity.

steps: Take a regular action of $G$ on $X$: it is transitive and every point has a trivial stabilizer.
Forget that the stabilizers are trivial.
The remaining condition says that $G$ has a single orbit on $X$.
So every regular action is transitive, but a transitive action can have large stabilizers.
links.why: Orbit-counting results for transitive groups also apply to regular actions.

reminder: The 2-adic valuation of a nonzero integer is the exponent of the highest power of 2 that divides it.
definition: The 2-adic valuation is the map $v_2$ on [rational numbers](c:rational-number) with $v_2(0)=\infty$ and $v_2(2^k a/b)=k$ for odd [integers](c:integer) $a,b$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. It satisfies $v_2(xy)=v_2(x)+v_2(y)$ and $v_2(x+y)\ge\min(v_2(x),v_2(y))$.
examples: Non-example: the number of ones in the binary form of $n$ is not $v_2(n)$, because $v_2(6)=1$ but $6=110_2$ has two ones.

steps: Take a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ and write a nonzero rational number as $p^k a/b$ with $p$ not dividing $a$ or $b$.
Set $v_p(x)=k$ and $v_p(0)=\infty$.
Choose the prime $p=2$.
Then $v_p$ is the 2-adic valuation $v_2$.
links.why: Every fact proved for the $p$-adic valuation holds for $v_2$ by setting $p=2$.

reminder: A 2-site is a 2-category with a choice of covering families that stay covering under pullback.
definition: A 2-site is a [2-category](c:2-category) equipped with a 2-coverage: for each object $U$, a choice of covering families of 1-morphisms into $U$ that can be refined along every pullback, where pullbacks are taken in the 2-categorical sense. It is the 2-categorical analogue of a [Grothendieck site](c:grothendieck-site) given by a [coverage](c:coverage).
examples: Every Grothendieck site, viewed as a 2-category with only identity 2-morphisms, is a 2-site.
Non-example: a 2-category with covering families that are lost under pullback of 1-morphisms is not a 2-site, because the stability condition fails.

steps: Take a Grothendieck site: a category $C$ with a coverage.
Regard $C$ as a 2-category whose only 2-morphisms are identities.
Pullbacks in $C$ are pullbacks in this 2-category, so the coverage stays stable under pullback.
So the site is a 2-site; a general 2-site drops the rule that all 2-morphisms are identities.
links.why: Ideas from sites carry over to 2-sites by checking that each step respects 2-morphisms.

reminder: A 3-grading splits a Lie algebra into three pieces of degree $-1$, $0$ and $1$, and the bracket adds degrees.
definition: A 3-grading of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ is a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) decomposition $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_{-1}\oplus\mathfrak{g}_0\oplus\mathfrak{g}_1$ with $[\mathfrak{g}_i,\mathfrak{g}_j]\subseteq\mathfrak{g}_{i+j}$, where $\mathfrak{g}_k=0$ for $|k|>1$. It is a [graded Lie algebra](c:graded-lie-algebra) structure that lives in the degrees $-1$, $0$ and $1$.
examples: The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has the 3-grading $\mathfrak{g}_{-1}=\langle f\rangle$, $\mathfrak{g}_0=\langle h\rangle$, $\mathfrak{g}_1=\langle e\rangle$, given by the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}(h/2)$.
In $\mathfrak{sl}_{p+q}$, the upper right block has degree $1$, the block diagonal has degree $0$, and the lower left block has degree $-1$.
Non-example: the grading of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ by root height has degrees from $-2$ to $2$ and $[\mathfrak{g}_1,\mathfrak{g}_1]\ne0$, so it is a 5-grading, not a 3-grading.

steps: Take a 3-grading $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_{-1}\oplus\mathfrak{g}_0\oplus\mathfrak{g}_1$.
Index the pieces by integers and put $\mathfrak{g}_k=0$ for all other $k$.
The rule $[\mathfrak{g}_i,\mathfrak{g}_j]\subseteq\mathfrak{g}_{i+j}$ then holds for all integers $i$ and $j$.
So $\mathfrak{g}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded Lie algebra, with the extra condition that only the degrees $-1$, $0$ and $1$ occur.
links.why: Results on graded Lie algebras apply to 3-gradings, which the Kantor-Koecher-Tits construction uses.

reminder: Absolute geometry is plane geometry built from Hilbert's axioms without any axiom about parallel lines.
definition: Absolute (or neutral) geometry is the geometry that follows from [Hilbert's axioms](c:hilbert-s-axioms) of incidence, order and [congruence](c:congruence-in-geometry), together with the [archimedean axiom](c:archimedean-axiom) where a theorem needs it, but without any axiom about [parallel lines](c:parallel-lines). Its theorems hold in both Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry.
examples: In absolute geometry, the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
The Saccheri-Legendre theorem holds in absolute geometry: the angle sum of a triangle is at most $180^\circ$.
Non-example: the statement that every triangle has angle sum exactly $180^\circ$ is not a theorem of absolute geometry, because it fails in the hyperbolic plane.

steps: Take the hyperbolic plane with its lines, order and congruence.
It satisfies every axiom of absolute geometry.
It adds the hyperbolic parallel axiom: through a point off a line pass at least two lines that miss the line.
So every theorem of absolute geometry holds in the hyperbolic plane.
links.why: A proof in absolute geometry works in both the Euclidean and the hyperbolic plane.

reminder: A map has acyclic fibres when every fibre is nonempty and has the cohomology of a point.
definition: A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ has acyclic fibres when each [fibre](c:fiber) $f^{-1}(y)$ is nonempty and acyclic: its [Cech cohomology](c:cech-cohomology) with coefficients in a group $G$ satisfies $H^0=G$ and $H^n=0$ for $n>0$.
examples: The projection $X\times[0,1]\to X$ has acyclic fibres, because the interval is contractible.
The map from the closed disc $D^n$ to a point has acyclic fibre $D^n$.
Non-example: the map from the circle $S^1$ to a point has no acyclic fibre, because $H^1(S^1)\ne0$.

steps: Take a map whose fibres are contractible spaces.
A contractible space is homotopy equivalent to a point.
Cohomology does not change under homotopy equivalence of reasonable spaces, so each fibre has the cohomology of a point.
So each fibre is acyclic; the converse fails, because an acyclic space need not be contractible.
links.why: A contractible-fibre hypothesis is enough for results stated for acyclic fibres.

reminder: The adic completion at $v$ is the completion of the field $K$ for its $v$-adic valuation.
definition: Let $R$ be a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain) with fraction field $K$, and let $v$ be a point of the [height-one prime spectrum](c:height-one-spectrum), that is, a nonzero prime ideal of $R$. The adic completion $K_v$ is the [completion](c:completion) of $K$ for the $v$-adic [discrete valuation](c:discrete-valuation), obtained by adding the limits of all Cauchy sequences.
examples: For $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and $v=(p)$, the adic completion is the field $\mathbb{Q}_p$ of [p-adic numbers](c:p-adic-number).
For $R=k[t]$ and $v=(t)$, the adic completion of $k(t)$ is the field $k((t))$ of [Laurent series](c:laurent-series).
Non-example: the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ for the usual absolute value is $\mathbb{R}$, which is not an adic completion, because that absolute value does not come from a prime ideal.

steps: Take $R=\mathbb{Z}$, so $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and $v=(p)$ for a prime $p$.
The $v$-adic valuation is the $p$-adic valuation.
The completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ for it is $\mathbb{Q}_p$.
So the $p$-adic numbers are the adic completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ at $p$, and the general case allows any Dedekind domain.
links.why: Statements about $\mathbb{Q}_p$ often extend to local fields at any prime of a Dedekind domain.

reminder: The affine Grassmannian of a group $G$ is the ind-scheme quotient of the loop group $G(k((t)))$ by $G(k[[t]])$.
definition: For an [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group) $G$ over a field $k$, the affine Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_G$ is the [ind-scheme](c:ind-scheme) whose $k$-points are $G(k((t)))/G(k[[t]])$. This is the quotient of the [loop group](c:loop-group) of [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) points by the subgroup of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) points, and it plays the role of a flag variety for the loop group.
examples: For $G=GL_n$, the $k$-points of $\mathrm{Gr}_G$ correspond to the $k[[t]]$-lattices in $k((t))^n$.
For the trivial group $G$, the affine Grassmannian is a single point.
Non-example: the ordinary Grassmannian of $k$-planes in $n$-space is a finite-dimensional projective variety, not a quotient of a loop group.

reminder: An algebraic function satisfies a nonzero polynomial equation whose coefficients are polynomials in the variable.
definition: A function $y=f(x)$ is algebraic when there is a nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) $P(x,y)$ in two variables with $P(x,f(x))=0$ for all $x$ in the domain of the [function](c:function) $f$.
examples: Every [rational function](c:rational-function) $p(x)/q(x)$ is algebraic, because it satisfies $q(x)y-p(x)=0$.
The function $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ is algebraic, because it satisfies $y^2-x=0$.
Non-example: $e^x$ is not algebraic, because no nonzero polynomial $P(x,y)$ gives $P(x,e^x)=0$.

steps: Take a rational function $f=p/q$ with $q$ nonzero.
Then $y=f(x)$ solves $q(x)y-p(x)=0$.
The polynomial $q(x)y-p(x)$ is nonzero.
So $f$ is an algebraic function; algebraic functions also include roots such as $\sqrt{x}$.
links.why: Rational functions are the algebraic functions of degree one in $y$.

reminder: An algebraic weak factorization system is a functorial factorization of morphisms given by a comonad and a monad on the arrow category.
definition: An algebraic weak factorization system on a category is a [functorial factorization](c:functorial-factorization) $f=Rf\circ Lf$ together with a [comonad](c:comonad) structure on $L$ and a [monad](c:monad) structure on $R$ on the [arrow category](c:arrow-category), related by a [distributive law](c:distributive-law). Its left maps are the maps that admit an $L$-coalgebra structure, and its right maps are the maps that admit an $R$-algebra structure.
examples: In the category of sets, the image factorization $f=(\text{inclusion of the image})\circ(\text{surjection onto the image})$ is functorial and gives an algebraic weak factorization system with idempotent $L$ and $R$.

Garner's algebraic small object argument applied to a set $I$ of maps in a locally presentable category gives an algebraic weak factorization system whose right maps are the maps with the right lifting property against $I$.
Non-example: a factorization $f=g\circ h$ chosen separately for each $f$, without functoriality, is not algebraic, because $L$ and $R$ are not functors.

steps: Take an algebraic weak factorization system $(L,R)$ on a category $C$.
Call a map left if it admits an $L$-coalgebra structure, and right if it admits an $R$-algebra structure.
Each map $f$ factors as $Rf\circ Lf$ with $Lf$ left and $Rf$ right.
Coalgebra and algebra structures give lifts, and retracts preserve them, so the two classes form a weak factorization system.
links.why: Every algebraic weak factorization system has an underlying weak factorization system with a functorial choice of factorizations.

steps: Take an orthogonal factorization system on $C$ whose factorizations are functorial.
Let $L$ and $R$ be its factorization functors, which are idempotent.
Unique lifting makes $L$ a comonad and $R$ a monad on the arrow category with the required distributive law.
So a functorial orthogonal factorization system is an algebraic weak factorization system with idempotent $L$ and $R$.
links.why: Orthogonal factorization systems are the case where the algebraic structure is unique.

reminder: An angle trisector is one of the two rays from the vertex of an angle that cut the angle into three equal angles.
definition: For an [angle](c:angle) $\angle ABC$, an angle trisector at $B$ is a ray $BD$ inside the angle with $\angle ABD=\tfrac13\angle ABC$ or $\angle ABD=\tfrac23\angle ABC$. Every angle has exactly two trisectors.
examples: The trisectors of a right angle make angles of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ with one side.
In Morley's theorem, the adjacent trisectors of the three angles of any triangle meet at the vertices of an equilateral triangle.
Non-example: the angle bisector is not a trisector, because it makes the angle $\tfrac12\angle ABC$ with the side $BA$.

reminder: Anti de Sitter spacetime is a hyperboloid in a flat space with two time directions, with the induced Lorentzian metric.
definition: Up to [isometry](c:isometry), the anti de Sitter spacetime $AdS_d$ of dimension $d$ is the [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $\mathbb{R}^{d-1,2}$ given by $x_1^2+\dots+x_{d-1}^2-x_0^2-x_d^2=-1$. It carries the [pseudo-Riemannian metric](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold) induced from the flat metric of signature $(d-1,2)$, which has signature $(d-1,1)$ and constant negative curvature.
examples: $AdS_2$ is the one-sheeted hyperboloid $x_0^2+x_2^2=1+x_1^2$ in $\mathbb{R}^{1,2}$ with its induced Lorentzian metric.
$AdS_3$ is the group $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ with the metric given by its Killing form.
Non-example: de Sitter spacetime is the hypersurface $x_1^2+\dots+x_d^2-x_0^2=1$ in Minkowski space, and it has positive curvature.

steps: Take $AdS_d$ with the metric induced from $\mathbb{R}^{d-1,2}$.
At each point, the tangent space is the orthogonal complement of a timelike vector, so the induced metric has signature $(d-1,1)$.
So $AdS_d$ is a Lorentzian manifold.
The extra condition is constant negative curvature, which makes it maximally symmetric.
links.why: General facts about Lorentzian manifolds apply to anti de Sitter spacetime.

reminder: For any two positive quantities $a$ and $b$, some whole multiple of $a$ exceeds $b$.
definition: The archimedean axiom says that for all positive elements $a$ and $b$ of an [ordered field](c:ordered-field), for example the lengths of two segments, there is a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ with $na>b$. It excludes infinitely large and infinitely small elements.
examples: The ordered fields $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ satisfy the archimedean axiom.
In Euclidean geometry, laying a short segment end to end enough times gives a segment longer than any given segment.
Non-example: the field $\mathbb{R}(x)$ of rational functions, ordered so that $x>n$ for every integer $n$, is not archimedean, because no multiple $n\cdot1$ exceeds $x$.

reminder: An arithmetic group is a subgroup of an algebraic group over the rationals that matches its integer points up to finite index.
definition: Let $G\subseteq GL_n$ be a [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, and put $G(\mathbb{Z})=G(\mathbb{Q})\cap GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$. A [subgroup](c:subgroup) $\Gamma\subseteq G(\mathbb{Q})$ is arithmetic when $\Gamma\cap G(\mathbb{Z})$ has finite index in both $\Gamma$ and $G(\mathbb{Z})$, where $GL_n$ is the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group).
examples: The group $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is an arithmetic subgroup of $SL_n(\mathbb{Q})$.
Every congruence subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, such as $\Gamma_0(N)$, has finite index in $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and so is arithmetic.
Non-example: the upper unitriangular integer matrices have infinite index in $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, so they are not arithmetic as a subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Q})$.

steps: Take $G=PGL_2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, with integer points $PGL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
The modular group $PSL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ has index $2$ in $PGL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
A subgroup of finite index in $G(\mathbb{Z})$ is arithmetic.
So the modular group is an arithmetic group.
links.why: The modular group is the model case that guides results on arithmetic groups.

reminder: An atlas of a manifold is a family of coordinate charts whose domains cover the manifold.
definition: An atlas of an $n$-dimensional [manifold](c:manifold) $X$ is a family of charts $(U_i,\varphi_i)$ such that the sets $U_i$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$, each $\varphi_i$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of $U_i$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the transition maps $\varphi_j\circ\varphi_i^{-1}$ are continuous. For a smooth atlas, the transition maps are [smooth](c:smooth-function).
examples: The circle $S^1$ has an atlas of two charts: the stereographic projections from the north pole and from the south pole.
The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ has an atlas with one chart, the identity map.
Non-example: one stereographic chart of the sphere $S^2$ is not an atlas, because it misses a point and so its domain does not cover $S^2$.

steps: Take an atlas $\{(U_i,\varphi_i)\}$ of $X$.
The domains $U_i$ are open subsets of $X$ that together cover $X$.
So $\{U_i\}$ is an open cover of $X$.
The atlas adds a chart on each $U_i$, with transition maps that agree on overlaps.
links.why: Every atlas gives an open cover, so covering arguments apply to the chart domains.

reminder: The attainable set of a control system is the set of states that a trajectory can reach from a given starting state.
definition: For a control system $\dot x=f(x,u)$ with controls $u\in U$ on a [manifold](c:manifold), the attainable set of a point $x_0$ is the set of all endpoints $x(T)$ with $T\ge0$ of solutions of the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) with $x(0)=x_0$ and an admissible control $u(\cdot)$. Fixing $T$ gives the attainable set at time $T$.
examples: For $\dot x=u$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $|u|\le1$, the attainable set from $0$ at time $T$ is the interval $[-T,T]$.
For $\dot x=1$ with no control, the attainable set from $x_0$ at time $T$ is the single point $x_0+T$.
Non-example: for $\dot x=u^2$, the number $-1$ is not in the attainable set of $0$, because $x$ never decreases.

reminder: An automorphism is an isomorphism from an object onto itself.
definition: An automorphism of an [object](c:object) $X$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) $f:X\to X$, that is, a morphism with a two-sided inverse $g:X\to X$ satisfying $gf=fg=\mathrm{id}_X$. The automorphisms of $X$ form a group under composition.
examples: An automorphism of a set is a bijection of the set onto itself, that is, a permutation.
The automorphisms of a vector space $V$ are the invertible linear maps $V\to V$.
Complex conjugation is an automorphism of the field $\mathbb{C}$.
Non-example: the doubling map $n\mapsto 2n$ is a group homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}$ to itself, but not an automorphism, because it has no inverse.

steps: Take an isomorphism $f:X\to Y$ with inverse $g$.
Require that $Y$ equals $X$.
Then $f$ and $g$ are maps from $X$ to $X$ with $gf=fg=\mathrm{id}_X$.
So $f$ is an automorphism of $X$.
links.why: An automorphism is an isomorphism whose source and target agree, so isomorphism results apply.

steps: Take the category of sets and a set $X$.
An isomorphism of sets is a bijection.
So an automorphism of $X$ is a bijection $X\to X$, which is a permutation.
Automorphisms of other structures are the permutations that also preserve that structure.
links.why: Permutations are the automorphisms of a bare set, and automorphisms extend them to every structure.

reminder: An axiomatization of a theory is a set of axioms from which every theorem of the theory follows.
definition: An axiomatization of a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) $T$ is a set $A$ of [axioms](c:axiom) in the language of $T$ whose logical consequences are exactly the sentences of $T$. It is finite when $A$ is finite, and recursive when a program can decide whether a sentence belongs to $A$.
examples: The axioms of associativity, a neutral element and inverses form a finite axiomatization of the first-order theory of groups.
Peano arithmetic has an infinite recursive axiomatization, with one induction axiom for each formula.
Non-example: associativity and a neutral element alone do not axiomatize group theory, because they do not prove that inverses exist.

reminder: The Borel transform sends an entire function $\sum a_n z^n$ to the series $\sum n!\,a_n w^{-n-1}$.
definition: For an [entire function](c:entire-function) $f$ of [exponential type](c:function-of-exponential-type) with [power series](c:power-series) $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nz^n$, the Borel transform is $F(w)=\sum_{n\ge0}n!\,a_n w^{-n-1}$, which converges and is holomorphic for $|w|$ large. By termwise integration, it equals the integral $\int_0^\infty f(z)e^{-wz}\,dz$ for $\operatorname{Re}w$ large, which is the [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) of $f$.
examples: For $f(z)=e^{az}$, the Borel transform is $1/(w-a)$.
For $f(z)=z^k$, the Borel transform is $k!/w^{k+1}$.
Non-example: $e^{z^2}$ is not of exponential type, and the series $\sum n!\,a_n w^{-n-1}$ for it diverges for every $w$.

steps: Take an entire function $f$ of exponential type and a number $w$ with $\operatorname{Re}w$ large.
Integrate the series of $f$ term by term against $e^{-wz}$ over $[0,\infty)$.
Each term gives $\int_0^\infty z^n e^{-wz}\,dz=n!/w^{n+1}$.
So the Laplace transform of $f$ equals the Borel transform of $f$ there.
links.why: The Borel transform is the Laplace transform of an entire function, written coefficient by coefficient.

reminder: The Brillouin torus of a crystal is the space of wave vectors taken modulo the reciprocal lattice.
definition: Let a crystal in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ have the translation lattice $\Lambda$ of its [crystallographic group](c:crystallographic-group). Its Brillouin torus is the quotient $\mathbb{R}^n/\Lambda^*$ of the space of wave vectors by the [dual lattice](c:dual-lattice) $\Lambda^*=\{k: k\cdot\lambda\in2\pi\mathbb{Z}\text{ for all }\lambda\in\Lambda\}$, which is an $n$-[torus](c:torus).
examples: For a one-dimensional crystal with lattice spacing $a$, the Brillouin torus is the circle $\mathbb{R}/(2\pi/a)\mathbb{Z}$.
For the square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, the Brillouin torus is $\mathbb{R}^2/2\pi\mathbb{Z}^2$, a 2-torus.
Non-example: the first Brillouin zone is a polygon with boundary, not a torus; it gives the torus only after points that differ by a reciprocal lattice vector are identified.

steps: Take the dual lattice $\Lambda^*$, a lattice of rank $n$ in the space $\mathbb{R}^n$ of wave vectors.
The quotient of $\mathbb{R}^n$ by a lattice of rank $n$ is homeomorphic to $(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^n$.
This quotient is the Brillouin torus, so it is an $n$-torus.
The extra data are that the lattice comes from a crystal and the points are physical wave vectors.
links.why: Topological facts about the $n$-torus, such as its cohomology, apply to the Brillouin torus.

reminder: A cartesian category is a category that has all finite products.
definition: A cartesian category is a [category](c:category) that has all finite [products](c:product), that is, a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) and a product $A\times B$ of every pair of objects.
examples: The category of sets is cartesian: the product is the cartesian product, and the terminal object is a one-point set.
The categories of groups and of topological spaces are cartesian.
Non-example: the category of fields is not cartesian, because it has no terminal object.

steps: Take a cartesian closed category $C$.
By definition $C$ has finite products.
Drop the condition that each functor $-\times A$ has a right adjoint.
What remains is a cartesian category, so every cartesian closed category is cartesian.
links.why: Results that use only finite products apply to every cartesian closed category.

steps: Take a cartesian category $C$ and choose a product $A\times B$ for each pair and a terminal object $1$.
Set $A\otimes B=A\times B$ and let $1$ be the unit.
The universal property of products gives the associator and unitors, and they satisfy the coherence laws.
So $C$ is a monoidal category, and even a symmetric one, whose tensor product is the categorical product.
links.why: A cartesian category is a monoidal category in which the tensor product is the product.

reminder: A finite group has characteristic 2 type when every 2-local subgroup has a 2-group as its generalized Fitting subgroup.
definition: A [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ is of characteristic 2 type when every 2-local subgroup $H$ of $G$ satisfies $F^*(H)=O_2(H)$, that is, the [generalized Fitting subgroup](c:generalized-fitting-subgroup) of $H$ is a 2-group. A 2-local subgroup is the [normalizer](c:normalizer) in $G$ of a nontrivial 2-subgroup, and a 2-subgroup is a [p-group](c:p-group) for $p=2$.
examples: The group $PSL_3(2)$ of order $168$ is of characteristic 2 type: its 2-local subgroups are $D_8$ and $S_4$, and each has a 2-group as generalized Fitting subgroup.
Simple groups of Lie type over a field of characteristic 2, such as $PSL_2(4)\cong A_5$, are the main examples.
Non-example: $A_7$ is not of characteristic 2 type, because the centralizer of $(12)(34)$ has a normal subgroup of order 3 generated by $(567)$, so its generalized Fitting subgroup is not a 2-group.

reminder: A chiral object differs from its mirror image, and no rotation turns one into the other.
definition: An object in Euclidean space is chiral when no orientation-preserving [isometry](c:isometry) maps it onto its mirror image, which is its image under a [reflection](c:reflection). In physics, the chirality of a [spinor](c:spinor) is its eigenvalue $\pm1$ under $\gamma_5$, which separates left-handed from right-handed fermions.
examples: A left hand is chiral, because no rotation or translation turns it into a right hand.
A helix, such as a corkscrew thread, is chiral.
Non-example: a sphere, or any figure with a mirror plane of symmetry, is not chiral, because its mirror image is the figure itself.

reminder: A co-Heyting algebra is a lattice whose order dual is a Heyting algebra.
definition: A co-Heyting algebra is a bounded [lattice](c:lattice) in which, for all $a$ and $b$, there is a smallest element $a\setminus b$ with $a\le b\vee(a\setminus b)$. Equivalently, its order dual is a [Heyting algebra](c:heyting-algebra).
examples: The closed subsets of a [topological space](c:topological-space) form a co-Heyting algebra, with $A\setminus B$ equal to the closure of the set difference.
Every [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) is a co-Heyting algebra, with $a\setminus b=a\wedge\neg b$.
Non-example: the open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ do not form a co-Heyting algebra, because no smallest open set $C$ satisfies $\mathbb{R}\subseteq(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})\cup C$.

steps: Take a Boolean algebra $B$ with complement $\neg a$.
Set $a\setminus b=a\wedge\neg b$.
Then $a\le b\vee c$ holds exactly when $a\wedge\neg b\le c$, so $a\wedge\neg b$ is the smallest such $c$.
So $B$ is a co-Heyting algebra, and a general co-Heyting algebra need not have complements.
links.why: Results for co-Heyting algebras hold in every Boolean algebra.

steps: Take a co-Heyting algebra $L$ with subtraction.
For each $b$, the rule $a\setminus b\le c$ exactly when $a\le b\vee c$ makes $b\vee-$ a right adjoint.
Right adjoints preserve meets, so $b\vee(c\wedge d)=(b\vee c)\wedge(b\vee d)$.
This is a distributive law, so $L$ is a distributive lattice.
links.why: Every tool for distributive lattices applies to co-Heyting algebras.

reminder: The boundary of an element $a$ of a co-Heyting algebra is $a\wedge(1\setminus a)$.
definition: In a [co-Heyting algebra](c:co-heyting-algebra) $L$, the boundary of $a$ is $\partial a=a\wedge\neg a$, where $\neg a=1\setminus a$ is the [co-Heyting negation](c:co-heyting-negation) of $a$.
examples: In the co-Heyting algebra of closed subsets of a space $X$, the boundary of a closed set $A$ is $A\cap\overline{X\setminus A}$, its topological boundary.
In a Boolean algebra, $\neg a$ is the complement of $a$, so $\partial a=a\wedge\neg a=0$ for every $a$.
Non-example: in a Heyting algebra, the intuitionistic negation satisfies $a\wedge\neg a=0$, so this formula gives no boundary there.

steps: Take a topological space $X$ and its co-Heyting algebra of closed sets.
For a closed set $A$, the element $1\setminus A$ is the closure of $X\setminus A$.
So $A\wedge(1\setminus A)$ is the set $A\cap\overline{X\setminus A}$.
For a closed set this is the topological boundary of $A$, so the algebraic boundary extends it.
links.why: The algebraic boundary gives a notion of boundary without an ambient space.

reminder: A coCartesian fibration of operads is a map of operads in which every morphism below has a coCartesian lift.
definition: Let $\mathcal{O}^\otimes$ be an [(infinity,1)-operad](c:infinity-1-operad). A coCartesian fibration of (infinity,1)-operads over $\mathcal{O}^\otimes$ is a map $p:\mathcal{C}^\otimes\to\mathcal{O}^\otimes$ of (infinity,1)-operads that is also a coCartesian fibration of simplicial sets: every morphism of $\mathcal{O}^\otimes$ lifts to a $p$-coCartesian morphism starting at any chosen object over its source.
examples: A symmetric monoidal (infinity,1)-category is a coCartesian fibration of (infinity,1)-operads $\mathcal{C}^\otimes\to\mathrm{Fin}_*$ over the commutative operad.
The identity map of an (infinity,1)-operad is a coCartesian fibration of (infinity,1)-operads.
Non-example: a map of operads that omits the target of some morphism out of an object in its image has no coCartesian lift for that morphism.

reminder: A coherent (infinity,1)-topos is an (infinity,1)-topos generated by quasi-compact coherent objects, so it behaves like a compact topos.
definition: An [(infinity,1)-topos](c:infinity-1-topos) is coherent when it is generated under colimits by coherent objects and its terminal object is coherent. An object is coherent when it is [quasi-compact](c:quasicompact-morphism), meaning that every covering by [effective epimorphisms](c:effective-epi) has a finite subfamily that still covers, and so are its diagonals.
examples: The (infinity,1)-topos of sheaves on a coherent topological space is coherent.
The etale (infinity,1)-topos of a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme is coherent.
Non-example: the (infinity,1)-topos of sheaves on the real line is not coherent, because its terminal object is not quasi-compact: the cover by the intervals $(-n,n)$ has no finite subcover.

steps: Take a coherent (infinity,1)-topos $X$.
By definition $X$ is an (infinity,1)-topos.
The extra condition is that $X$ is generated by coherent objects and its terminal object is coherent.
This makes $X$ compact in the sense of finite subcovers.
links.why: A coherent (infinity,1)-topos is an (infinity,1)-topos with a finiteness condition, so general topos tools apply.

reminder: A coherent space is a topological space that is homeomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring.
definition: A coherent (or spectral) space is a [topological space](c:topological-space) that is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to the underlying space of the [spectrum of a commutative ring](c:spectrum-of-a-commutative-ring) with its Zariski topology. Intrinsically, it is quasi-compact and [sober](c:sober-topological-space), and its quasi-compact open sets form a base that is closed under finite intersections.
examples: The prime spectrum of $\mathbb{Z}$ is coherent: it has one closed point for each prime and one generic point $(0)$.
Every Stone space, and every finite $T_0$ space, is coherent.
Non-example: the closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact and Hausdorff but not coherent, because its only quasi-compact open sets are $\emptyset$ and $[0,1]$, which do not form a base.

steps: Take a Stone space $X$: a compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected space.
It is sober, because every Hausdorff space is sober.
Its quasi-compact open sets are the clopen sets, which form a base closed under finite intersections.
So $X$ is coherent, and a coherent space need not be Hausdorff.
links.why: Duality results for Stone spaces extend to coherent spaces by dropping the Hausdorff condition.

steps: Take a coherent space $X$ and a homeomorphism from $X$ to $\operatorname{Spec}A$.
Every irreducible closed subset of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ has the form $V(\mathfrak{p})$ for a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$.
So it has the unique generic point $\mathfrak{p}$, and homeomorphisms preserve generic points.
Hence every irreducible closed subset of $X$ has a unique generic point, and $X$ is sober.
links.why: A coherent space is sober, so points are recovered from the closed sets.

reminder: A comodule algebra is an algebra with a coaction of a bimonoid that is a morphism of algebras.
definition: Let $B$ be a [bimonoid](c:bimonoid) (a bialgebra) in a symmetric monoidal category. A right $B$-comodule algebra is a [monoid](c:monoid) $A$ with a right coaction $\rho:A\to A\otimes B$ that makes $A$ a [comodule](c:comodule) and is a morphism of monoids, where $A\otimes B$ has the tensor product monoid structure.
examples: Every bialgebra $B$ is a $B$-comodule algebra over itself, with the coaction given by the comultiplication $\Delta$.
For a group $G$, a comodule algebra over the group algebra $\mathbb{k}[G]$ is a $G$-graded algebra $A=\bigoplus_g A_g$ with $A_gA_h\subseteq A_{gh}$.
Non-example: the algebra $k[x]/(x^2-x)$ with $x$ placed in degree $1$ of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is a graded vector space but not a graded algebra, because $x\cdot x=x$ has the wrong degree.

steps: Take a $B$-comodule algebra $(A,\rho)$.
Forget the multiplication of $A$.
The map $\rho:A\to A\otimes B$ still satisfies coassociativity and the counit law, so $A$ is a $B$-comodule.
A comodule algebra is a comodule with a multiplication that the coaction respects.
links.why: Statements about comodules apply to the underlying comodule of a comodule algebra.

reminder: A compact subspace is a subset such that every cover of it by open sets has a finite subcover.
definition: A subset $K$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a compact subspace when $K$ with the subspace topology is a [compact space](c:compact-space). Equivalently, every family of open sets of $X$ whose union contains $K$ has a finite subfamily whose union still contains $K$.
examples: A closed bounded interval $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}$ is a compact subspace, by the Heine-Borel theorem.
Every finite subset of every topological space is a compact subspace.
Non-example: the open interval $(0,1)$ is not a compact subspace of $\mathbb{R}$, because the cover by the sets $(1/n,1)$ has no finite subcover.

steps: Take a compact subspace $K$ of a space $X$.
Give $K$ the subspace topology.
Open sets of $K$ are the sets $U\cap K$ with $U$ open in $X$, so open covers of $K$ come from $X$.
Each such cover has a finite subcover, so $K$ is a compact space in its own right.
links.why: A compact subspace is a compact space that sits inside a larger space.

reminder: A compactification of a space $X$ is a compact space that contains $X$ as a dense subspace.
definition: A compactification of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [compact space](c:compact-space) $C$ together with an [embedding](c:embedding) $i:X\to C$ whose image is a [dense subspace](c:dense-subspace) of $C$. So $X$ is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to a dense subspace of $C$.
examples: The one-point compactification of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the sphere $S^n$.
The closed interval $[0,1]$ is a compactification of the open interval $(0,1)$.
Non-example: $[0,1]\cup\{2\}$ is compact and contains $(0,1)$, but $(0,1)$ is not dense in it, because $2$ is an isolated point.

reminder: A composition factor of a module is a simple quotient between two consecutive terms of a composition series.
definition: Let $M$ be a [module](c:module) with a [composition series](c:composition-series) $0=M_0\subset M_1\subset\dots\subset M_n=M$, in which each quotient $M_{i+1}/M_i$ is a [simple module](c:is-simple-module). The modules $M_{i+1}/M_i$ are the composition factors of $M$; by the Jordan-Holder theorem, they do not depend on the series, up to isomorphism and order.
examples: The $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}/6$ has the composition series $0\subset2\mathbb{Z}/6\subset\mathbb{Z}/6$, with composition factors $\mathbb{Z}/3$ and $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
A simple module is its own only composition factor.

Non-example: in the series $0\subset\mathbb{Z}/4$, the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/4$ is not simple, so it is not a composition factor; the series $0\subset2\mathbb{Z}/4\subset\mathbb{Z}/4$ has the composition factors $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

reminder: A set of points is concyclic when all its points lie on one sphere and in one plane.
definition: A set $S$ of points in a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) is concyclic when it is cospherical, so all its points have the same distance to some center, and coplanar, so all its points lie in one plane. Equivalently, $S$ lies on one [circle](c:circle).
examples: Any three distinct points that are not collinear are concyclic, because they lie on their circumcircle.
The four vertices of a rectangle are concyclic.
Non-example: the four vertices of a regular tetrahedron are cospherical but not coplanar, so they are not concyclic.

reminder: Points are concyclic when they all lie on one circle.
definition: Points $P_1,\dots,P_k$ of the plane are concyclic when some [circle](c:circle) passes through all of them, that is, when they all have the same distance $r>0$ from some center.
examples: The vertices of a regular polygon are concyclic, because each vertex has the same distance to the center of the polygon.
Any three points that are not collinear are concyclic: they lie on their circumcircle.

Non-example: the points $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(2,2)$ are not concyclic, because the circle through the first three has center $(1/2,1/2)$ and radius $\sqrt2/2$, and $(2,2)$ lies farther from the center.

reminder: A conformal map between Riemannian manifolds multiplies the metric by a positive function, so it preserves angles.
definition: A [smooth map](c:smooth-function) $f:X_1\to X_2$ between [Riemannian manifolds](c:riemannian-manifold) $(X_1,g_1)$ and $(X_2,g_2)$ is conformal when $f^*g_2=r^2g_1$ for a smooth function $r:X_1\to(0,\infty)$. Because the factor $r^2$ is positive, $f$ preserves the angles between tangent vectors.
examples: A similarity $x\mapsto\lambda Ox+b$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, with $O$ orthogonal and $\lambda>0$, is conformal with constant factor $r=\lambda$.
A holomorphic function $f$ with $f'\ne0$ is conformal for the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{C}$, with $r=|f'|$.
Non-example: the map $(x,y)\mapsto(2x,y)$ stretches only one direction, so it changes angles and is not conformal.

steps: Take an isometry $f:(X_1,g_1)\to(X_2,g_2)$, so $f^*g_2=g_1$.
Set $r\equiv1$, which is a smooth positive function.
Then $f^*g_2=r^2g_1$, so $f$ is conformal.
A conformal map replaces the rigid length condition by a free scale factor $r$.
links.why: Every isometry is conformal, so conformal results hold for isometries.

steps: Take a conformal map $f$ with $f^*g_2=r^2g_1$.
At each point, $df$ is $r$ times a linear isometry, so it sends round spheres to round spheres.
So the ratio of the largest to the smallest stretching of $df$ is $1$ everywhere.
Hence $f$ is $K$-quasiconformal with $K=1$, and quasiconformal maps allow larger $K$.
links.why: Conformal maps are the rigid case of quasiconformal maps, with dilatation exactly one.

reminder: A connective spectrum has trivial homotopy groups in all negative degrees.
definition: A connective spectrum is a [spectrum object](c:spectrum-object) $S$ whose [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) vanish in all negative degrees: $\pi_n(S)=0$ for every $n<0$.
examples: The [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) $\mathbb{S}$ is connective, with $\pi_0(\mathbb{S})=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_n(\mathbb{S})=0$ for $n<0$.
The [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) of an abelian group is connective, because its only nonzero homotopy group sits in degree $0$.
Non-example: periodic complex K-theory $KU$ is not connective, because $\pi_n(KU)=\mathbb{Z}$ for every even $n$, including negative $n$.

steps: Take a connective spectrum $S$.
Forget that its negative homotopy groups vanish.
What remains is a spectrum object, so $S$ is a spectrum.
links.why: General results on spectra apply to connective spectra.

steps: Take the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HA$ of an abelian group $A$.
Its only nonzero homotopy group is $\pi_0(HA)=A$.
So $\pi_n(HA)=0$ for all $n<0$, and $HA$ is connective.
links.why: Eilenberg-MacLane spectra are the simplest connective spectra, with one homotopy group.

reminder: A constructible sheaf is locally constant of finite type on each piece of a finite decomposition of the space.
definition: Let $X$ be a noetherian scheme with its [etale site](c:etale-site). A [sheaf](c:sheaf) $F$ of abelian groups on $X$ is constructible when $X$ has a finite partition into locally closed subsets $X_i$ such that each restriction $F|_{X_i}$ is a [locally constant sheaf](c:locally-constant-sheaf) with finite stalks.
examples: The constant sheaf $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ is constructible, using the trivial partition with the single piece $X$.
For an open subset $U\subset X$, the extension by zero of $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ from $U$ is constructible: it is constant on $U$ and zero on $X\setminus U$.

Non-example: on the affine line over a field, the direct sum of skyscraper sheaves $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ at all closed points is not constructible, because its stalk is nonzero at each closed point and zero at the generic point.

steps: Take a locally constant sheaf $F$ with finite stalks on a noetherian scheme $X$.
Use the trivial partition of $X$ with the single piece $X$.
The restriction of $F$ to $X$ is $F$ itself, which is locally constant.
So $F$ is constructible, and constructible sheaves also allow jumps between pieces.
links.why: Results for constructible sheaves apply to every locally constant sheaf with finite stalks.

reminder: A sequence converges to $x$ when it eventually lies in every neighborhood of $x$.
definition: A [sequence](c:sequence) $(x_n)$ in a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ converges to a point $x$ when for every [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) $U$ of $x$ there is an $N$ with $x_n\in U$ for all $n\ge N$. The same idea defines the limit of a [net](c:net), with eventually taken in the index set, and of a [filter](c:filter), which converges to $x$ when it contains all neighborhoods of $x$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$, the sequence $1/n$ converges to $0$.
In a space with the trivial topology, every sequence converges to every point, so limits need not be unique.

Non-example: the sequence $(-1)^n$ does not converge in $\mathbb{R}$, because it does not stay eventually inside a small neighborhood of $1$ or of $-1$, and every other point has a neighborhood that misses all terms.

steps: Take a topological space $X$ with its neighborhood filters $\mathcal{N}(x)$.
Say that a filter $\mathcal{F}$ converges to $x$ when $\mathcal{F}$ contains $\mathcal{N}(x)$.
A sequence converges to $x$ exactly when its filter of tails converges to $x$ in this sense.
This relation satisfies the axioms of a convergence space, which does not need open sets.
links.why: Topological convergence is one case of convergence in a convergence space.

reminder: A covering system is a finite set of congruence classes whose union is the set of all integers.
definition: A covering system is a finite family of [congruence](c:congruence) classes $a_i\bmod n_i$ with $i=1,\dots,k$ such that every [integer](c:integer) lies in at least one class, that is, $\mathbb{Z}=\bigcup_i(a_i+n_i\mathbb{Z})$. Each class is a [coset](c:coset) of the subgroup $n_i\mathbb{Z}$, and the family is exact when every integer lies in exactly one class.
examples: The classes $0\bmod2$ and $1\bmod2$ form an exact covering system.
The classes $0\bmod2$, $0\bmod3$, $1\bmod4$, $5\bmod6$ and $7\bmod12$ form a covering system with distinct moduli, found by Erdos.
Non-example: the classes $0\bmod2$ and $1\bmod4$ do not cover $\mathbb{Z}$, because the integer $3$ lies in neither.

reminder: A cyclic polygon is a polygon whose vertices all lie on one circle.
definition: A cyclic polygon is a [polygon](c:polygon) whose vertices are [concyclic](c:concyclic-points), that is, all lie on one [circle](c:circle), which is called its circumcircle.
examples: Every triangle is a cyclic polygon, because three points that are not collinear lie on a circumcircle.
Every regular polygon is cyclic, and so is every rectangle.
Non-example: a rhombus that is not a square is not cyclic, because a cyclic parallelogram must be a rectangle.

steps: Take a cyclic polygon $P$.
Forget the circle through its vertices.
What remains is a polygon, so every cyclic polygon is a polygon.
A cyclic polygon adds the condition that all its vertices are concyclic.
links.why: Facts about polygons hold for cyclic polygons, which add a circumcircle.

steps: Take a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, a quadrilateral whose vertices lie on one circle.
A quadrilateral is a polygon with four vertices.
So $ABCD$ is a polygon whose vertices are concyclic.
Hence $ABCD$ is a cyclic polygon with four sides.
links.why: Cyclic quadrilaterals are the four-sided case of cyclic polygons.

reminder: Three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory is a gauge theory on 3-manifolds whose action is the integral of the Chern-Simons form.
definition: For a compact [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ and a level $k$, $D=3$ Chern-Simons theory assigns to a [connection](c:connection) $A$ on a trivial [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) over a closed oriented 3-manifold $M$ the action $S(A)=\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_M\mathrm{CS}(A)$, the integral of the [Chern-Simons form](c:chern-simons-form) $\mathrm{CS}(A)=\operatorname{tr}(A\wedge dA+\tfrac23A\wedge A\wedge A)$. For a nontrivial bundle, one extends the bundle over a 4-manifold to define the action.
examples: For $G=SU(2)$ and level $k$, the expectation values of Wilson loops of a knot give the Jones polynomial, by Witten.
For $G=U(1)$, the action is $\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_MA\wedge dA$.
Non-example: the Yang-Mills action $\int|F|^2$ depends on a metric, but the Chern-Simons action does not, so Yang-Mills theory is not Chern-Simons theory.

steps: Take the gauge group $G=U(1)$, so a connection is a real-valued 1-form $A$.
The term $A\wedge A\wedge A$ vanishes, because $A\wedge A=0$ for a single 1-form.
The action becomes $\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_MA\wedge dA$.
This is the abelian Chern-Simons action, so the abelian theory is the case $G=U(1)$.
links.why: The abelian theory is the simplest case of the three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory, with no cubic term.

reminder: Dehn filling glues a solid torus to a torus boundary of a 3-manifold along a chosen slope.
definition: Let $M$ be a compact orientable [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) with a torus boundary component $T$, and let $s$ be a slope, which is the isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T$. The Dehn filling $M(s)$ is the 3-manifold that results from gluing a [solid torus](c:solid-torus) to $M$ along $T$ by a homeomorphism that sends the meridian of the solid torus to $s$.
examples: Filling the complement of the unknot in $S^3$, which is a solid torus, along the meridian slope of the knot gives back $S^3$.
Filling the complement of the unknot along the longitude slope gives $S^2\times S^1$.
Non-example: gluing a solid torus to a boundary component that is a sphere or a surface of genus $2$ is not a Dehn filling, because the boundary must be a torus.

steps: Take a knot $K$ in $S^3$ and a slope $p/q$ on the boundary of a tubular neighborhood of $K$.
Remove the open tubular neighborhood to get the knot complement $M$, a 3-manifold with torus boundary.
Dehn surgery on $K$ with slope $p/q$ glues back a solid torus whose meridian goes to the slope $p/q$.
That is the Dehn filling $M(p/q)$ of the knot complement.
links.why: Dehn filling extends surgery on knots to any 3-manifold with a torus boundary.

reminder: A double category has objects, horizontal and vertical morphisms, and squares that compose in both directions.
definition: A double category is an [internal category](c:internal-category) in the category $\mathbf{Cat}$ of small [categories](c:category). Concretely, it has objects, horizontal morphisms, vertical morphisms and squares, with a horizontal and a vertical composition of squares that satisfy the interchange law.
examples: For a [2-category](c:2-category) $K$, take the objects of $K$, the 1-morphisms as horizontal morphisms, only identities as vertical morphisms, and the 2-morphisms as squares.
The commutative squares in a category $C$ form a double category, with composition of squares side by side and one above the other.
Non-example: a family of squares that compose horizontally but not vertically is not a double category, because both compositions must exist and satisfy the interchange law.

steps: Take the category $\mathbf{Cat}$ of small categories, which has pullbacks.
An internal category in $\mathbf{Cat}$ has a category $D_0$ of objects and a category $D_1$ of morphisms, with source, target, identity and composition functors.
The objects and morphisms of $D_0$ become the objects and vertical morphisms of a double category.
The objects and morphisms of $D_1$ become its horizontal morphisms and squares, and functoriality of composition gives the interchange law.
links.why: A double category is an internal category in $\mathbf{Cat}$, so internal category tools apply.

steps: Take a strict 2-category $K$.
Let the horizontal morphisms be the 1-morphisms of $K$ and let the only vertical morphisms be identities.
Then a square is a 2-morphism of $K$ between its top edge and its bottom edge.
The two compositions of squares are the two compositions of 2-morphisms, and the interchange law carries over.
links.why: Every 2-category is a double category with trivial vertical morphisms.

reminder: The Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HA$ of an abelian group $A$ has $A$ as its only homotopy group, in degree $0$.
definition: For an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $A$, the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HA$ is the [spectrum](c:spectrum-object) whose $n$-th space is the [Eilenberg-MacLane space](c:eilenberg-maclane-space) $K(A,n)$, with structure maps $K(A,n)\to\Omega K(A,n+1)$ that are weak equivalences. Its [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) are $\pi_0(HA)=A$ and $\pi_n(HA)=0$ for $n\ne0$.
examples: The spectrum $H\mathbb{Z}$ represents integral cohomology: $H^n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is a group of maps from the suspension spectrum of $X$ to $\Sigma^nH\mathbb{Z}$.
The spectrum $H\mathbb{F}_2$ represents cohomology with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/2$.
Non-example: the sphere spectrum $\mathbb{S}$ is not an Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum, because it has nonzero homotopy groups in many degrees, such as $\pi_0=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_1=\mathbb{Z}/2$.

steps: Take the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HA$ of an abelian group $A$.
Its only nonzero homotopy group is $\pi_0(HA)=A$.
So $\pi_n(HA)=0$ for all $n<0$.
Hence $HA$ is a connective spectrum whose homotopy is concentrated in degree $0$.
links.why: Results for connective spectra apply to $HA$, which is the simplest connective example.
